newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania urged to do more to lift coffee quality.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania urged to do more to lift coffee quality.

text.p: The quality of Tanzanian coffee has improved significantly over the past year, but more needs to be done if the country is to compete with the world's top quality producers, industry officials and traders said.

Despite a decline in output in recent years, the quality of mild Tanzanian arabica from the northern highlands around Mount Kilimanjaro had returned prices at the New York auctions only exceeded by Kenya and Colombia, they said.
But low world prices, high output costs and taxes that accounted for about 30 percent of farm income had stifled the incentive for Tanzanian growers to improve quality.
"It is very difficult...without high prices the farmers loose interest in the crop," Edward Sannda, managing director of the Tanzanian Coffee Board (TCB), told Reuters in Moshi.

Sannda said the board aimed to see Tanzania's mild arabicas competing with Kenya's, and was setting up a training workshop for farmers on quality improvement and another for traders on marketing promotion.

Jeremy Lefroy, managing director of the African Coffee Co., said, "What matters is the smallholders are doing something there. Quality is not going down. It is improving...but you certainly have to do more work than they (farmers) do today."
He added, "I believe the standard of production has gone down and the farmers know less than in past times -- you cannot blame the world market for everything."
Another trader said that while replanting was not the only solution to increased quality, it was an important part of the process to ensure full sector recovery.
"Despite the trees being so old, we are still rubbing shoulders with Kenya," he said.
"We are trying to do our best to provide basic inputs. As private buyers we are playing many roles, offering free inputs, technical advice," the trader added.
Rasik Doshi, an official with the Tanzanian Coffee Growers Association, which represents 92 smallholders and estates, said more inputs were required.
"But the problem is the financing. The money the growers generate from coffee sales is not enough to buy new seedlings and machinery and the government is not cooperative.

"They (government) have put too many taxes on coffee. Coffee on a small scale is not profitable. The cost of coffee cultivation is very high in terms of water and chemicals and the farmers get more from other agricultural products."
Lefroy said the government had to consider reducing taxes that were imposed when world prices peaked.

"Lower taxes, replanting and training is needed. The coffee in Tanzania is basically grown by the poorest people in the country, but the coffee farmers are some of the most heavily taxed people here," said Lefroy.
